title: Troubleshoot Your Cluster Directly from Kyma Dashboard with Terminal
author: Damian_Badura
text:
Troubleshoot Your Cluster Directly from Kyma Dashboard with Terminal 
 Troubleshooting applications running in Kubernetes often requires switching between tools, creating temporary resources, and preparing the environment before you can even start investigating the actual problem. To simplify this experience, Kyma dashboard (Busola) will introduce a new Terminal feature on October 6, 2026. It will provide direct, browser-based access to your cluster and include common troubleshooting tools such as curl, jq, and yq, allowing you to start debugging immediately without creating temporary workloads or installing additional utilities. Why We Built It 
 If you've worked with Kubernetes applications, you've probably encountered situations where you needed to verify connectivity, inspect service configuration, or debug networking issues between workloads. 

 A common workflow is to create a temporary Pod, install debugging tools, and only then start investigating the issue. While this approach works, it adds extra steps before troubleshooting can begin. 

 With the new Terminal feature, you can execute commands directly from within the cluster and focus on solving the problem instead of preparing the environment. 

 A Practical Example 
 Let's walk through a common troubleshooting scenario in Kubernetes: a Service that appears to be running correctly but is not reachable. 
 We'll deploy a simple Pod and Service, use the built-in Terminal to verify connectivity, identify the root cause, and validate the fix directly from Kyma dashboard. 

 Step 1: Create Test Resources 
 In Kyma dashboard, choose Upload YAML and apply the following configuration: 
 apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
 name: my-test-env
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
 namespace: my-test-env
 name: nginx
 labels:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: my-api
spec:
 containers:
 - name: nginx
 image: nginx
 ports:
 - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
 name: my-service
 namespace: my-test-env
spec:
 selector:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: my-nginx
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 80
 targetPort: 80 This creates: 
 a namespace called 
 my-test-env 
 an nginx Pod 
 a Service intended to expose the Pod Step 2: Navigate to the Namespace and Check the Pod Status 
 Open the command palette: (macOS: Cmd + K , Windows/Linux: Ctrl + K ), type ns/my-test-env , and press Enter. 
 To navigate to your nginx Pod open the command palette and type pods/nginx. Press Enter. 
 If the Pod status shows Running , your application is up. 

 Step 3: Verify Pod Connectivity 
 From the Pod details page, note the Pod IP address shown in the Status card. 
 Open the Terminal and run: 
 curl -I ${YOUR_POD_IP} You should receive a response containing HTTP/1.1 200 OK . 
 This confirms that the Pod itself is reachable and serving requests. 

 Step 4: Test the Service 
 Now let's verify whether the Service is correctly configured. 
 Open the command palette and navigate to svc/my-service 

 You can call Kubernetes Services either through their ClusterIP or their DNS name. For real applications, it's recommended to use the DNS name, and this is how we proceed in this example. 
 Open the Terminal and execute: 
 curl -I my-service.my-test-env.svc.cluster.local Instead of a successful response, you'll receive a connection error. 
 At first glance, this might look like a networking problem. However, the Pod itself was reachable in the previous step. Thanks to the built-in Terminal, we were able to quickly verify Pod connectivity and narrow the scope of the problem to the communication between the Service and its target Pods. 

 Finding the Root Cause 
 Looking closer at the Service configuration, the issue becomes clear. 
 The Pod has the label: 
 app.kubernetes.io/name: my-api But the Service selector expects: 
 app.kubernetes.io/name: my-nginx Because the labels don't match, the Service cannot find any target Pods and therefore has no endpoints available. 
 This is a common Kubernetes misconfiguration and a perfect example of a problem that's easy to diagnose from the built-in Terminal. 

 Fixing the Service 
 Upload the updated YAML from the Cluster Overview page. 
 apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
 name: my-service
 namespace: my-test-env
spec:
 selector:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: my-api
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 80
 targetPort: 80 2. Once the Service is updated, return to the Terminal and run: 

 curl -I my-service.my-test-env.svc.cluster.local This time, you should receive an HTTP/1.1 200 OK response . 

 The Service can now successfully route traffic to the Pod. 

 Faster Troubleshooting Out of the Box 
 This simple example demonstrates the value of the new Terminal feature. With a single click, you gain access to a browser-based terminal connected directly to your cluster. There's no need to create temporary Pods or install utilities manually. You can immediately start investigating problems and validating fixes. 

 Try It Out 
 The Terminal feature is designed to make troubleshooting faster, more convenient, and more accessible directly from Kyma dashboard. 
 Give it a try and let us know what you think. We'd love to hear how you're using the Terminal and which troubleshooting scenarios it helps you solve. Feel free to share your feedback or create an issue in the Busola repository . 
 And if you'd like to stay up to date with the latest Kyma features and releases, make sure to subscribe to the What's New page.

title: Implementing Change Logs in RAP on SAP BTP ABAP Environment
author: Gayathri_Vedagiri
text:
I had a requirement in one of my RAP applications to display the change history of a business object. 
 The Change Log needed to show the field name, old value, new value, changed by, changed date/time, and the action performed. 
 I checked the available options and decided to use the Change Document Object instead of creating a separate custom table for maintaining the history. 
 In this post, I will share how I configured the Change Document Object in SAP BTP ABAP Environment, connected it with the RAP behavior definition, and displayed the change history using a RAP Custom Entity and Query Provider. 
 Create Change Document Object 
 I created the Change Document Object in ADT and added the required table and fields. 

 Add Change Documents in Behavior Definition 
 After creating the Change Document Object, I added it to the RAP behavior definition. 
 changedocuments master (ZCHANGE_LOG_OBJECT) 

 { 

 changedocuments( 

 create:key, 

 update:data, 

 delete:none 

 ); 

 } 
 create:key is used for creation, while update:data is used to capture the changed data. Delete logging was not required for this scenario. 
 Change Document Data Element 
 In ADT, open the relevant data element and enable the Change Document / Change Document Logging setting for the data element. 
 I missed this initially, and the field was not being recorded in the Change Document data even though the Change Document Object and behavior definition were configured. 
 After enabling change logging for the required data elements and regenerating the Change Document Object, the field changes were available in the Change Document data. 
 RAP Custom Entity 
 To display the Change Log in the application, I created a RAP Custom Entity. 
 @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_CHANGE_LOG_QUERY' 

 define custom entity ZI_CHANGE_LOG 

 { 
 key ChangeDocNumber : abap.char(10); 
 key ChangeDocItem : abap.char(70); 
 key FieldName : abap.char(50); 
 @UI.hidden: true 
 BusinessObjectId : abap.char(90); 
 @UI.hidden: true 
 ChangedDate : abap.dats; 
 @UI.hidden: true 
 ChangedTime : abap.tims; 
 ChangedOn : abap.char(20); 
 ChangedBy : abap.char(12); 
 OldValue : abap.string; 
 ` 
 NewValue : abap.string; 

 Action : abap.char(20); 

 } 
 Query Provider 
 The query provider implements: 
 ABAP CLASS 
 INTERFACES if_rap_query_provider. 
 The main logic is inside: 
 abap 
 METHOD if_rap_query_provider~select. 
 DATA(lo_filter) = io_request->get_filter( ). 
 IF lo_filter IS BOUND. 
 DATA(lt_ranges) = lo_filter->get_as_ranges( ). 
 LOOP AT lt_ranges INTO DATA(ls_name_range). 
 CASE ls_name_range-name. 
 WHEN 'BUSINESSOBJECTID'. 
 LOOP AT ls_name_range-range 
 INTO DATA(ls_object_range). 
 IF ls_object_range-sign = 'I' 
 AND ls_object_range-option = 'EQ'. 
 lv_object_id = ls_object_range-low. 
 ENDIF. 
 ENDLOOP. 
 ENDCASE. 
 ENDLOOP. 
 ENDIF. 
 I use the business object ID so that the query only reads the change history belonging to the current object. 
 Reading Change Documents 
 cl_chdo_read_tools=>changedocument_read( 
 EXPORTING 
 i_objectclass = 'ZCHANGE_LOG_OBJECT' 

 it_objectid = lt_objid 

 IMPORTING 

 et_cdredadd_tab = lt_redadd 

 CHANGING 

 ct_cdhdr = lt_cdhdr 

 ). 
 The header and item data are then mapped to the Custom Entity. 
 ls_result-ChangedDate = ls_hdr-udate. 

 ls_result-ChangedTime = ls_hdr-utime. 

 ls_result-ChangedBy = ls_hdr-username. 

 ls_result-ChangeDocNumber = ls_item-changenr. 

 ls_result-ChangeDocItem = ls_item-tabkey. 

 ls_result-FieldName = ls_item-fname. 

 ls_result-OldValue = ls_item-value_shstr_old. 

 ls_result-NewValue = ls_item-value_shstr_new. 

 CASE ls_item-chngind. 
 WHEN 'I'. 
 ls_result-Action = 'Created'. 
 WHEN 'U'. 
 ls_result-Action = 'Changed'. 

 WHEN 'D'. 
 ls_result-Action = 'Deleted'. 
 ENDCASE. 

 Sorting and Paging 
 I also handled sorting so that the latest changes are displayed first. 
 SORT lt_result BY 

 ChangedDate DESCENDING 

 ChangedTime DESCENDING 

 ChangeDocNumber DESCENDING 

 ChangeDocItem DESCENDING. 
 Paging is handled using the RAP request paging information. 
 Result 
 Finally, the Change Log is displayed in the Fiori application. 

 The result shows the field, old value, new value, action, user and date/time. 
 Conclusion 
 That's how I implemented the Change Log for my RAP application in the SAP BTP ABAP Environment. 
 The Change Document Object handles the change information, and I used CL_CHDO_READ_TOOLS to read it and expose it through the RAP Custom Entity. 
 Hope this helps if you are working on a similar requirement.

title: Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas
author: MostafaElbarbary
text:
Agent Ready Data Series : 
 01 From AI Ready Data to Agent Ready Data 
 02 Is a Data Product Ready for an AI Agent 
 03 Data Products Need Owners Not Only Schemas 

 When a customer says a data product is ready, I like to ask who will answer when an agent gives the wrong answer. The schema may be clear and the pipeline may run every day. But if a business definition changes or a source starts arriving late, somebody must own that change. 

 Figure: The owner remains accountable for changes and exceptions after a data product is published. 
 Treat the interface as a product 
 Take a supplier performance data product. Its consumers may include a dashboard, a sourcing analyst and an agent that recommends which supplier needs attention. Each consumer needs to know the unit of analysis, refresh schedule, permitted use, expected quality and contact for an issue. A table name and column list tell only part of that story. 
 I would define a small product agreement: business purpose, owner, source systems, grain, measure definitions, freshness target, quality rules, sensitivity and access method. I would also describe what happens when the schema or a business rule changes. These are design choices for the team that publishes and consumes the data, not properties I would assume exist automatically. 
 The agent changes the support model 
 A human analyst may notice a missing country or an unusual supplier name and investigate. An agent might continue to the next step before anyone notices. That makes ownership and change communication more urgent. If a quality rule fails, should the agent stop, answer with a warning or route the case to a person? The data product owner and process owner should decide together. 
 SAP Business Data Cloud provides a data product approach, and the catalog helps users find and inspect the assets available to them. My recommendation is to add a clear operating agreement around each high-value product used by agents. Start with one use case, test the agreement with its consumers, then reuse what works in the next domain. 
 The strongest sign of a mature data product is not that it has been published. It is that a consumer knows what it means, whether it can be trusted today and who will resolve an issue tomorrow. 
 This also changes how I measure success. I would track whether consumers can find the product, understand its scope and resolve an issue without a long chain of emails. An agent pilot is a good stress test because it exposes unclear ownership quickly. 
 The product owner should also hear how the agent is being used. If users repeatedly ask questions the product cannot answer, that is input for the product roadmap. If an agent frequently stops because a field arrives late, the owner can prioritize that issue with the source team. Consumption feedback should improve the product.

title: Implementing Workflow for Bank Account Management in SAP S/4HANA
author: Dinesh_Murugesan19
text:
Introduction 
 Bank accounts are critical master data in any organization. Changes to bank account information can have a direct impact on payment processing, cash management, and financial operations. Because of this, organizations often require an approval mechanism before newly created or modified bank account information becomes effective. 
 In SAP S/4HANA, Bank Account Management provides functionality to maintain bank account master data through the Manage Bank Accounts Fiori application. SAP also provides workflow capabilities that can be used to introduce an approval process for bank account creation and changes. 
 In this blog, I will walk through the configuration approach for implementing a workflow for Bank Account Management, starting from the basic settings and number ranges and ending with the requester and approver experience. 
 The objective is not only to explain the configuration but also to show how the different configuration components work together to create an end-to-end approval process. 
 Business Scenario 
 Consider a scenario where a finance user needs to create a new bank account or modify an existing bank account. 
 Instead of allowing the change to become effective immediately, the organization wants the following process: 
 Requester 
 → Creates or modifies the bank account 
 → Submits the request 
 → Workflow is triggered 
 → Approver receives the request 
 → Approver reviews the details 
 → Approves or rejects the request 
 → Requester monitors the final status 
 This provides a controlled process for maintaining bank account master data. 
 The standard process covered in this scenario uses the following Fiori applications: 
 Manage Bank Accounts – Used to create and maintain bank account details. 
 Manage Workflow for Bank Admin – Used to manage the bank account workflow. 
 My Sent Requests for Bank Accounts – Used by the requester to monitor submitted requests. 
 My Inbox – Used by the approver to process workflow items. 
 The complete process flow is also reflected in the configuration document used for this implementation. 
 Configuration Overview 
 The workflow implementation consists of several configuration activities. 
 The major configuration areas are: 
 Define Basic Settings 
 Define Number Ranges for Change Requests 
 Define Number Ranges for Bank Account Technical IDs 
 Assign Number Ranges 
 Define Settings for Bank Account Master Data 
 Maintain Event Type Linkage for Workflow 
 Define Responsibilities for Workflow Rules 
 Configure and manage the workflow in Fiori 
 The configuration sequence is important because the different settings work together to determine when a workflow is triggered and who is responsible for approving it. 
 Define Basic Settings 
 The first step is to maintain the basic settings required for Bank Account Management. 
 The configuration can be accessed through: 
 SPRO → Financial Supply Chain Management → Cash and Liquidity Management → General Settings → Define Basic Settings 

 This establishes the basic framework required for Bank Account Management. 
 Before proceeding with the workflow-specific configuration, it is important to ensure that the required basic settings are available in the system. 
 Define Number Ranges for Change Requests 
 Once the basic settings are maintained, the next step is to define the number range for bank account change requests. 
 When a user creates or modifies bank account information and submits it for approval, a change request is generated. 
 The number range provides the identification mechanism for these requests. 
 Therefore, a properly configured number range is required before the workflow process can be tested end to end. 

 Define Number Ranges for Bank Account Technical IDs 
 The next configuration activity is to define the number range for Bank Account Technical IDs . 
 The technical ID is used by the system to uniquely identify the bank account master record. 
 This is separate from the business-facing bank account number. 
 Therefore, both number range concepts need to be considered when configuring Bank Account Management: 
 Change Request Number Range 
 Bank Account Technical ID Number Range 

 Assign Number Ranges 
 After defining the required number ranges, the next step is to assign them appropriately. 
 This ensures that the system can generate the required identifiers when bank account master data and change requests are created. 

 At this stage, it is useful to perform a basic validation to make sure the number ranges are correctly assigned before moving into the workflow-specific configuration. 

 Define Settings for Bank Account Master Data 
 This is one of the important configuration steps in the workflow design. 
 Here, we can define: 
 Which account types are relevant for the workflow 
 Which fields should be considered for workflow processing 
 Which changes should trigger an approval process 
 For example, an organization may decide that only specific bank account types require workflow approval. 
 The configuration also allows relevant fields to be considered for workflow processing. 
 If a configured field is changed or modified, the corresponding change document can trigger the workflow approval process. 
 Why is this important? 
 Not every change to a bank account necessarily needs to be treated in the same way. 
 By defining the relevant account types and fields, organizations can create a more controlled workflow process around sensitive bank master data. 

 Maintain Event Type Linkage 
 After defining the bank account master-data settings, the next important step is maintaining the event type linkage used to trigger the workflow. 
 The event linkage connects the relevant bank account event with the workflow process. 
 Conceptually, the process works like this: 
 Bank Account Change 
 ↓ 
 Relevant Event 
 ↓ 
 Workflow Trigger 
 ↓ 
 Approval Request 
 This is the point where the master-data change becomes connected to the workflow process. 

 The event type linkage configuration is therefore an important bridge between Bank Account Management and SAP Business Workflow. 

 Define Responsibilities for Workflow Rules 
 After configuring the workflow trigger, we need to determine who should approve the request . 
 This is handled through the responsibility/rule configuration. 
 The approving person or responsible agent can be maintained according to the organization's workflow design. 
 For example, an organization could design the approval responsibility based on: 
 Company Code 
 Bank Account Type 
 Organizational responsibility 
 Business role 
 Other business-specific rules 
 The important point is that the workflow should not only be triggered successfully; it should also determine the correct approver. 
 In the configuration used for this scenario, the responsibility configuration is where the approving person is established. 

 Manage Workflow for Bank Accounts in Fiori 
 Once the backend configuration is completed, the workflow can be managed through the relevant Fiori application. 
 The Manage Workflow for Bank Admin application provides the business-facing layer for maintaining the workflow process. 
 This is where the configured workflow can be reviewed and managed according to the organization's approval requirements. 
 At this point, the technical configuration and the business approval design come together. 

 End-to-End Process 
 Now let's look at the complete process from a business user's perspective. 
 Step 1 – Create or Change Bank Account 
 The requester opens: 
 Manage Bank Accounts 
 The user creates a new bank account or modifies relevant information in an existing bank account. 
 Step 2 – Submit the Request 
 Once the required information has been maintained, the requester submits the request for workflow approval. 
 Based on the configuration, the system identifies whether the change requires workflow approval. 
 Step 3 – Workflow Is Triggered 
 If the change satisfies the configured workflow conditions, the workflow is triggered automatically. 
 The request then moves into the approval process. 
 Step 4 – Requester Monitors the Request 
 The requester can use: 
 My Sent Requests for Bank Accounts 
 to monitor the request. 
 This provides visibility into the current workflow status. 
 The requester does not have to depend on separate communication to determine whether the request has been processed. 
 Step 5 – Approver Receives the Request 
 The designated approver receives the workflow item in: 
 My Inbox 
 The approver can review the bank account information and perform the appropriate action. 
 The available business action depends on the workflow design and configuration. 
 Step 6 – Workflow Completion 
 After the approver processes the request, the requester can monitor the updated status through My Sent Requests for Bank Accounts . 
 The request can move through statuses such as: 
 Pending → Approved / Rejected → Completed 
 The exact status flow can depend on the configured workflow scenario. 
 This end-user monitoring flow is also documented in the configuration material. 
 Process Flow at a Glance 
 The complete process can be summarized as: 
 MANAGE BANK ACCOUNTS 
 │ 
 ▼ 
 Create / Modify Bank Account 
 │ 
 ▼ 
 Submit Request 
 │ 
 ▼ 
 Workflow Triggered 
 │ 
 ▼ 
 Determine Approver 
 │ 
 ▼ 
 MY INBOX 
 │ 
 ┌───────┴───────┐ 
 ▼ ▼ 
 Approve Reject 
 │ │ 
 └───────┬───────┘ 
 ▼ 
 Workflow Status 
 │ 
 ▼ 
 MY SENT REQUESTS 
 This makes it easier to understand the relationship between the requester, workflow engine, approver, and bank account master data. 
 What Happens When a Bank Account Is Changed? 
 One of the key aspects of this configuration is that the workflow does not necessarily need to be treated as a completely separate process from bank account maintenance. 
 Instead, the workflow can be connected to relevant changes in bank account master data. 
 For example: 
 User changes a configured field 
 ↓ 
 System identifies the relevant change 
 ↓ 
 Change request is generated 
 ↓ 
 Workflow is triggered 
 ↓ 
 Approver receives the request 
 This provides a controlled mechanism for managing sensitive bank account changes. 
 Key Configuration Takeaways 
 From an implementation perspective, there are several important areas to validate. 
 Number ranges 
 Make sure both change request and bank account technical ID number ranges are correctly defined and assigned. 
 Account types 
 Clearly identify which bank account types should participate in the workflow. 
 Relevant fields 
 Determine which bank account fields should trigger approval when changed. 
 Event linkage 
 Validate that the relevant event is correctly linked to the intended workflow. 
 Approver determination 
 The workflow must be able to identify the correct responsible approver. 
 Fiori applications 
 Validate the complete business process using: 
 Manage Bank Accounts 
 Manage Workflow for Bank Admin

title: SAP HANA Cloud Expands Availability on SAP Sovereign Cloud — What It Means for Regulated Customers
author: isomesan
text:
In the September 2026 edition of What’s New in SAP HANA Cloud , we announced availability in two new SAP Sovereign Cloud regions, released during the Q3 2026 timeframe. With this expansion, SAP HANA Cloud is now available across the Five-Eyes countries, Europe/Germany, and India , addressing customer demand for digital sovereignty in additional geographies. 
 SAP HANA Cloud availability on SAP Sovereign Cloud and SAP NS2 

 This blog highlights two significant milestones: the new availability in Europe/Germany and the new FedRAMP certification at SAP NS2 in the United States with SAP NS2. 
 Now Available to Highly Regulated European Customers 
 Europe/Germany is the first deployment of SAP Sovereign Cloud in Europe. It brings SAP’s sovereign solutions to organizations with elevated regulatory and security requirements — those that typically cannot adopt SAP’s public cloud offering. SAP HANA Cloud is among the solutions available in this landscape at launch. 
 A Fully Sovereign, SAP-Owned Foundation 
 The Europe/Germany deployment runs on SAP Cloud Infrastructure, an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) platform developed by SAP and based on open-source technologies. By owning and operating every layer — from infrastructure to application — SAP enables sovereignty across the full technology stack. 
 Key characteristics include: 
 Independent from third-party cloud providers: The environment runs on SAP’s own infrastructure. 
 A sovereign region of SAP Cloud Infrastructure: The region is hosted in SAP-owned data centers in Walldorf and St. Leon-Rot. In June 2026, SAP received Authorization to Use from the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) to process information classified as VS-NfD ("Restricted — For Official Use Only") on SAP Cloud Infrastructure in these data centers. 
 Data residency in Germany : All data, including telemetry, remains in Germany. 
 Local operations : Administration and maintenance are handled by security-cleared personnel based in Germany. 
 A locally hosted control plane : The control plane remains within the region, supporting technical sovereignty. 
 A European legal entity : The service is provided by SAP SE. 
 Together, these characteristics give highly regulated European organizations a way to adopt SAP HANA Cloud while meeting their sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements. 
 Now Ready for Adoption by U.S. Federal Civilian Agencies 
 SAP HANA Cloud at SAP NS2 has achieved FedRAMP Moderate certification and is now available to U.S. federal civilian agencies through the SAP NS2 Government Cloud. 
 This U.S.-based cloud environment, delivered by SAP NS2, meets stringent U.S. security and compliance requirements. It runs on AWS GovCloud, is managed exclusively by U.S. citizens, and all operations and data are restricted to U.S. soil. 
 SAP HANA Cloud has been generally available at SAP NS2 since 2025 , serving commercial customers in regulated industries, such as Defense Industrial Base (DIB) and utility providers. The FedRAMP certification now extends access to U.S. federal civilian agencies seeking to build secure, compliant, data-driven applications. 
 Learn more about SAP HANA Cloud at SAP NS2 . 
 What This Means for Customers 
 For highly regulated enterprises and public sector organizations, these milestones help address a long-standing trade-off between cloud innovation and digital sovereignty. Whether running on SAP Sovereign Cloud in Europe, or in the FedRAMP-certified SAP NS2 environment in the U.S., customers can process their sensitive data and analytics workloads in sovereign settings — with control across the data, operational, technical, and legal dimensions — while benefiting from the in-memory speed, elastic cloud scalability, and continuous innovation of SAP HANA Cloud. 
 -- Thanks to Marc Ng from SAP and Joshua Kuhn, Ashley Jennings, and Ayveri Lane from SAP NS2 for reviewing this post.

title: SAP IBP Response & Supply: ein Vorsprung, den kein anderer einholt
author: MarkusA
text:
SAP IBP Response & Supply: ein Vorsprung, den kein anderer einholt 
 Auftragsbasierte Supply-Planung, native SAP S/4HANA-Ausführung und der Weg zur autonomen Lieferkette 
 Das Wichtigste in Kürze 
 SAP IBP Response & Supply plant auf einzelnen Aufträgen und schreibt sie über Real-Time-Integration direkt nach SAP S/4HANA zurück —kein anderes Planungstool leistet so eine Reaktionsfähigkeit. 
 Mit den letzten 2026-Releases (2602 / 2605 / 2608) wird dieser Vorsprung weiter ausgebaut: harmonisiertes Szenariomanagement, AI- unterstüte Szenarioplanung mit Joule , Merkmalsbasierte Planung mit Haltbarkeit, Lieferantrengesteuerte Bestandsführung (VMI), Intelligente Deployment Conversion, Lieferpläne sowie Qualitätsprüflose zeigen die tiefe Integration mit der Execution. 
 Dasselbe Fundament macht agentische , autonome Supply-Planung real statt zur Demo: ein Agent, der auf echten Aufträgen handeln kann — kontrolliert und nachvollziehbar — innerhalb des Design-to-Operate-Prozesses von SAP. 
 Die meisten Supply-Chain-Planungstools beantworten die Frage „Wie viel sollen wir nächsten Monat produzieren?" SAP IBP Response & Supply beantwortet eine wertvollere Frage mit dem Kunden im Mittelpunkt: „Dieser konkrete Kundenauftrag wird sich um drei Tage verspäten — hier ist der genaue Grund, und was jetzt zu tun ist." 
 Das ist der Unterschied zu all dessen, was Response & Supply schwer kopierbar macht — und die 2026-Releases (SAP IBP 2602, 2605 und 2608) bauen diese Alleinstellungsmerkmale von SAP IBP Response & Supply weiter aus. 
 ________________________________________ 
 Inhalt 
 1 Das Fundament — Auftragsbasierte Planung und native SAP S/4HANA-Integration 
 2 Die Gamechanger — Was 2026 den Vorsprung zementiert hat 
 3 Ausblick — Der Weg zur autonomen Supply Chain 
 ________________________________________ 

 Das Fundament: Auftragsbasierte Planung und native SAP S/4HANA-Integration 
 Wettbewerbsvorsprung durch eng auftragsbasierte Planung eng verzahnt mit der Ausführung 
 Viele Supply-Chain-Planungstools planen in Zeitrastern und aggregierten Mengen . Dieser Ansatz hat echte Stärken — und SAP IBP bietet ihn nativ an: SAP IBP Time Series Supply Planning ist gezielt für Organisationen gemacht, die eine aggregierte Sicht wollen, bei der die Planung auf Perioden- und Gesamtmengenebene genau die richtige Flughöhe ist. Doch wenn eine Störung eintritt, können aggregierte Zahlen nur sagen, dass ein Bucket zu knapp ist. Sie können nicht sagen, welcher Auftrag gefährdet ist, welcher Kunde betroffen ist oder welche einzelne Restriktion der Auslöser ist. 
 Hier kommt das neue SAP IBP Datenmodell ins Spiel. Beide Engines laufen auf demselben einheitlichen Datenmodell — denselben Planungsbereichen, Stammdaten und Kennzahlen — sodass es kein Abgleich zwischen getrennten Tools notwendig ist. Kunden wählen für jeden Teil ihres Netzwerks die passende Flughöhe oder kombinieren beide, vollständig innerhalb einer Plattform. SAP IBP Response & Supply plant auf der Ebene einzelner Aufträge — Fertigungsaufträge, Bestellungen, Umlagerungen und Kundenaufträge. Zwei Eigenschaften die einen strukturellen Vorteil schaffen: 
 1. Granularität auf Auftragsebene. Jedes Planungsergebnis lässt sich auf ein reales Auftragsobjekt abbilden. Ein Planer kann eine verspätete Lieferung bis zum exakten geplanten Zugang und dem exakten Material zurückverfolgen, das sie ausbremst. 
 2. Native SAP S/4HANA-Integration — keine Middleware. Response & Supply liest und schreibt reale SAP-Ausführungsobjekte direkt über Echtzeit-Integration. Planaufträge fließen zurück nach SAP S/4HANA und werden ausgeführt, ohne ETL-Schichten oder nächtliche Batch-Brücken. Kein Planungsanbieter kann das ohne erhebliche Integrationsaufwand erreichen — denn sie integrieren zu SAP, während SAP IBP selbst SAP ist . Und nativ zu SAP S/4HANA bedeutet nicht nur für SAP: SAP IBP nimmt über Integrationsframework mit offenen APIs Daten aus Nicht-SAP-ERPs und externen Quellen auf — heterogene Multi-ERP-Landschaften werden damit unterstützt, auch ohne tiefe Ausführungsanbindung an SAP S/4HANA. 
 Alles Folgende erweitert dasselbe Prinzip: präzise planen und das Ergebnis direkt an die Ausführung übergeben. 
 ________________________________________ 
 Zwei Differenzierungsmerkmale auf diesem Fundament 
 Ursachenanalyse auf Auftragsebene. Weil die Planung auf realen Aufträgen über die mehrstufige Stückliste hinweg stattfindet, kann ein Planer die Restriktion hinter einem konkreten verspäteten Auftrag genau bestimmen, statt auf einen aggregierten Fehlbestand zu starren. Das ist der Unterschied zwischen einem Nachmittag Recherche und einer Zwei-Minuten-Entscheidung. 
 Transport Load Builder (TLB). TLB fasst Deployment-Anforderungen zu optimierten Transportladungen zusammen, die reale Kapazitätsrestriktionen berücksichtigen — Gewicht, Volumen sowie Fahrzeug-/Palettengrenzen — und rundet sie auf volle LKW- oder Container-Mengen, damit Planer keine halbleeren LKW losschicken oder eine Route überbuchen. Entscheidend: TLB ist kein separates Optimierungs-Silo, sondern sitzt direkt auf auftragsbasiertem Deployment und nativer SAP S/4HANA-Ausführung — der Fluss läuft also ununterbrochen von der Supply-Entscheidung → zum Ladeplan → zur ausgeführten Lieferung. Eigenständige Ladeplanungs-Tools gibt es; was ihnen fehlt, ist diese nahtlose Linie von der Supply-Entscheidung auf Auftragsebene bis zum beladenen LKW, in einem System. 
 ________________________________________ 
 Planner Workspace als zentrales Planungscockpit 
 Eine berechtigte Kritik an Enterprise-Planungssuiten — SAP eingeschlossen — war lange eine Anwendererfahrung der Planer, die über zu viele Bildschirme verteilt ist. SAP hat massiv investiert, um dem zu begegnen: Die Response-&-Supply-Oberflächen konvergieren zu Planner Workspaces als einem einzigen Planungs-Cockpit — einem One - Stop -Arbeitsplatz zum Erkennen, Entscheiden und Handeln. Auftragsprüfung, projizierter Bestand, Deployment, Engpassanalyse und Szenarioplanung leben zunehmend in einem konfigurierbaren Workspace, sodass ein Planer vom Erkennen eines Problems über das Simulieren einer Reaktion bis zum Freigeben der Aufträge kommt — ohne zwischen unverbundenen Apps zu springen. Weniger Kontextwechsel, eine konsistente Oberfläche. Und mit eingebettetem Joule erhält dieses Cockpit einen einzigen natürlichsprachigen Einstiegspunkt über diese Aufgaben hinweg — genau dort, wo der Planer arbeitet, bittet er die KI zu handeln. → Demo: Planner Workspaces – In-Focus Alerts (1:28) 
 ________________________________________ 
 Die Gamechanger: Was 2026 den Vorsprung zementiert hat 
 AI-Assisted Scenario Planning, auf harmonisiertem Szenariomanagement 
 SAP IBP 2602 führte harmonisiertes Szenariomanagement ein — ein einheitliches Szenariomodell, das Aufträge *und* Kennzahlen vereint, mit vollständigem Lebenszyklus (Anlegen, Ändern, Übernehmen) in Planner Workspaces, Simulationen, die auf Auftragsszenarien aufsetzen, verlängerten Szenariolaufzeiten, Übernahmeoptionen, die nun auch die Auftragsübernahme umfassen, und kontrolliertem Shine-Through, das nun Aufträge abdeckt. → Demo: Harmonized Scenario Management (3:23) → Release-Blog: SAP IBP 2602 
 SAP IBP 2608 setzt Joule als AI- Assisted Scenario Planning auf dieses Fundament. Per natürlicher Sprache kann ein Planer, der auf einen Lieferantenausfall reagiert, Joule bitten, die Auswirkung des Ausfalls bis hinunter zur Primärnachfrage zu bewerten, Aufträge für den betroffenen Lieferanten zu löschen, diesen Lieferanten von Planungsläufen auszuschließen und neuen Supply aus alternativen Quellen anzulegen — aus einer mehrstündigen manuellen Untersuchung wird ein geführter Dialog. Weil Szenarien auf realen Aufträgen operieren, zeigt der KI-Vergleich, welche konkreten Kundenaufträge jede Reaktion schützt oder opfert — nicht nur ein aggregiertes Service-Level-Delta. → Demo: AI-Assisted Scenario Planning (5:09) → Release-Blog: SAP IBP 2608 
 Merkmalsbasierte Planung für Prozess-, Pharma-,und Nahrungsmittelindustrie 
 Planung auf SKU-Ebene reicht nicht, wo zwei Chargen des „gleichen" Produkts nicht austauschbar sind. SAP IBP 2602 kombinierte Characteristics -Based Planning mit Shelf Life Planning : Haltbarkeit nach Merkmalen definieren, Verfallsdaten von Planungselementen wie Beständen berücksichtigen und die richtige Charge durch Bewertung von Merkmalen und Restlaufzeit auswählen — direkt auf Abfallreduktion und regulatorische Compliance in Food und Pharma ausgerichtet. SAP IBP 2608 ergänzte auch den SAP-Best-Practices-Content für CBP (auf Planungsbereich I_SAPSAP IBP2, mit Prozess-/Konfigurations-/Test-Assets), sodass Bedarfe mit Merkmalen nur von passendem Supply erfüllt werden. Nur sehr wenige Planungsplattformen leisten das nativ. 
 Lieferantrengesteuerte Bestandsführung (SAP IBP 2605) 
 SAP IBP 2605 führte Vendor Managed Inventory mit automatisierter Wiederbeschaffungsplanung ein. Statt dass der Kunde die Wiederbeschaffung anstößt, plant und triggert sie der Lieferant: Kundenbedarf und Bestandstransparenz speisen den SAP IBP-Supply-Planungslauf, Wiederbeschaffungsaufträge fließen automatisch über Echtzeit-Integration ins ERP, und ausnahmebasierte Alerts melden Probleme, ohne den automatisierten Fluss zu stören. Eine Koordinationsübergabe, die normalerweise in Tabellen und EDI lebt, geht in derselben auftragsbasierten Engine auf. → Demo: Vendor-Managed Inventory (3:42) → Release-Blog: SAP IBP 2605 
 VMI ist zugleich ein Brückenkopf in ein Thema, das Analysten und Wettbewerber stark gewichten — mehrstufige Lieferantenkollaboration . Zusammen mit dem SAP Business Network reicht auftragsbasierte Planung über die Unternehmensgrenzen hinaus: Prognose-, Bestell- und Bestandssignale lassen sich mit Lieferanten upstream teilen, sodass der Plan widerspiegelt, was Partner tatsächlich zusagen können, statt einer internen Annahme. 
 Intelligent Deployment Conversion (SAP IBP 2602) 
 Ein neuer Deployment-Conversion-Algorithmus wandelt Umlagerungsanforderungen automatisch in Deployment-Anforderungen um und nutzt dabei ausschließlich verfügbaren Supply (verfügbarer Bestand, geplante Zugänge). Er wandelt nach Bedarfstermin-Priorität um — das Dringendste zuerst — mit konfigurierbaren Bedarfs-/Supply-Horizonten, Rückversatz-Handling für überfällige Elemente, Einbezug fixierter STRs und Splitting von STRs bei Teilverfügbarkeit unter Wahrung von Rundungswerten. Es ist das Stück, das aus einem machbaren Supply-Plan konkrete, ausführbare Aufträge macht — der natürliche Zulauf zu TLB und Ausführung. → Demo: Deployment Conversion Run (4:34) 
 Tiefere Integration in die native Ausführung (SAP IBP 2608) 
 Drei Supply-Erweiterungen bauen den Vorsprung weiter aus, indem sie reale SAP S/4HANA-Ausführungssignale in die auftragsbasierte Planung einbeziehen: 
 Qualitätsprüflose integrieren in Echtzeit aus ECC/SAP S/4HANA als neuer SAP IBP-Auftragstyp, sodass in der Prüfung gebundener Bestand (mit erwarteten Freigabedaten und -mengen) in Planungsläufen berücksichtigt wird. 
 Beschaffungs-Lieferpläne bringen MM-Einteilungen über RTI in SAP IBP. Im SAP IBP werden Kundenbedarf gegen bestätigte Einteilungen zugeordnet und reduzieren so die Nervosität im Plan. 
 Zeitabhängige Ausbeute lässt Ausbeuteraten während der Stücklistenauflösung je Planungsperiode variieren — relevant für Halbleiter, Pharma, Food & Beverage, Chemie und diskrete Fertigung. → Demo: Time-Dependent Output Coefficient (3:34) 
 ________________________________________

title: From Inbox to Folder: Fetching Gmail Attachments with SAP Build Process Automation
author: RanjeetKr
text:
Connecting SAP Build Process Automation to Google Workspace, so invoice PDFs arriving in a Gmail inbox land in a local folder, ready for extraction and approval. 
 Introduction 
 This is the fourth post in the series. In the first post , we built the core invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation (BPA). In the second , we connected to a trial Document AI instance, and in the third , we wired extraction straight into the approval process. Throughout, the invoice PDFs were simply sitting in a folder, put there by hand. 
 In practice, invoices arrive by email. So in this post we remove that last manual step: a task automation connects to Google Workspace, searches a Gmail inbox for invoice emails, and saves the PDF attachments into a folder on the machine running the Desktop Agent. That folder is then what the extraction and approval flow reads from. 
 Here's what we'll cover: 
 Creating an OAuth 2.0 Client ID in Google Cloud Console 
 Creating the External Authentication in BPA Control Tower 
 Registering the authentication on the Desktop Agent and giving consent 
 Building a task automation that searches Gmail and downloads attachments 
 Testing it with a real email 
 Choosing How to Connect to Google Workspace 
 BPA offers a few ways to authorize against Google Workspace. Authorize Google (OAuth Client ID) and Authorize Google (Service Account) are activities placed inside the automation, and both work on Desktop Agent 2 and 3. Select Google Authentication works differently: the OAuth client is configured once in Control Tower, registered once on the Desktop Agent, and the automation simply selects it by name. 
 We'll use Select Google Authentication , which requires Desktop Agent 3 (SAP documents version 3.16 or higher for Google external authorization). No credentials live inside the automation itself, which keeps the project clean. 
 Step 1: Set Up the OAuth Client in Google Cloud Console 
 Everything starts on the Google side. Open the Google Cloud Console and select the project you want to work in. Under APIs & Services, the Credentials page shows the OAuth consent screen, the Create credentials button, and any OAuth 2.0 Client IDs already created. 

 APIs & Services > Credentials in the selected Google Cloud project. 
 Enable the APIs. Under Enabled APIs & services, enable the Google Workspace APIs you plan to use. I enabled the Gmail API, Google Calendar API and Google Drive API. Only Gmail is used in this post, but the others save a trip back later. 
 Configure the OAuth consent screen. On the Branding page of Google Auth Platform, give the app a name (mine is SAP-BPA-Test, which is what users see when they sign in) and a user support email. 

 Branding --- app name and user support email. 
 Scroll down to the app domain fields and the developer contact email. The domain fields (home page, privacy policy, terms of service) can stay empty for a testing setup. 

 Branding, continued --- app domain, authorized domains and developer contact information. 
 Set the Audience. I chose the External user type and left the publishing status as Testing. While in Testing, only listed test users can authorize the app, so add your own Gmail address under Test users. 

 Audience --- External user type, Testing status, and the test user list. 
 Add scopes under Data Access. Scopes define what the app is allowed to do with the account. I added userinfo.email, cloud-platform, calendar, drive and the Gmail scope ( https://mail.google.com/ ). Google groups Drive and Gmail under restricted scopes, which is why they get a stricter consent flow. 

 Data Access --- the non-sensitive, sensitive and restricted scopes added to the app. 
 Create the client. Under Clients, create a new OAuth client with the application type Desktop app. I named mine Desktop Agent BPA. Google generates a Client ID and a Client secret, and you can also download them as a clientid.json file. Control Tower needs exactly these two values. 

 The Desktop client --- Client ID and client secret (sensitive parts hidden). 
 Treat the client secret like a password, and keep it out of screenshots and source control. 
 Step 2: Create the External Authentication in Control Tower 
 Now we move to SAP Build. From the Lobby, open Control Tower > External Authentication. This is where BPA stores the OAuth client details for the tenant. The screenshot below already shows one entry, Google Workspace Test, along with the Create New Authentication button. 

 Control Tower > External Authentication. 
 Choose Google as the type of external portal, then enter a unique Name (this is the name you'll select in the automation later) and an optional Description. 
 Paste the Client ID and Client Secret from the Google client (the clientid.json values). 
 Select the scopes. User Email is pre-selected and mandatory. The list also offers Calendar, Cloud Platform, Drive and Gmail. I selected only Gmail for now, so the consent screen stays short and the permissions stay minimal. You can always create another authentication later with more scopes. 

 The Create Authentication dialog for Google. 
 Step 3: Register It on the Desktop Agent 
 The authentication exists on the tenant, but it isn't usable until the Desktop Agent on your machine registers it. 
 In the Desktop Agent, click the Settings gear and choose External Authentication. 

 Desktop Agent --- Settings > External Authentication. 
 The tenant's authentications are listed with their type and status. Open the one you created. 

 The external authentication listed in the Desktop Agent. 
 Enter the email address of the Google account to use. You can mark the authentication as Default, so automations fall back to it when no name is given. Once it shows Registered, it can also be unregistered from this same screen. 

 The registered authentication, with the email address hidden. 
 Registering opens Google's sign-in flow in the browser. The first screen confirms which account is signing in to the app we named on the Branding page. 

 Sign in with Google --- confirming the account for SAP-BPA-Test. 
 The second screen lists what the app wants to access, which here is the Gmail permission we selected in Control Tower. Because the app is in Testing and unverified, Google's wording is a bit more cautious. Review it and click Continue. 

 The consent screen requesting Gmail access. 
 That's the whole one-time setup. Any automation running on this Desktop Agent can now use the registered Google account. 
 Step 4: Build the Task Automation 
 With authorization in place, we can build the automation itself. I added a task automation, InvoiceApprovalAutomation, to the same project that holds the invoice approval process. For this post the flow is deliberately small: authenticate, search the inbox, clean the target folder, download the attachments, and log the result. 
 The Test Email 
 To test, I sent myself an email with a recognizable subject, Gmail-BPA, and three invoice PDFs attached. The automation searches for exactly that subject, so it only picks up emails meant for it. 

 The test email in the Gmail inbox --- three PDF attachments, ready to be read by the Desktop Agent. 
 Building the Flow 
 Select Google Authentication. The first activity takes the name of the external authentication as its only input. Pick the one you registered (in my case, Google Workspace Test). If it's left empty, the default registered authentication is used. The activity can throw a GoogleAuthError. 

 Select Google Authentication --- the name of the registered external authentication. 
 Try / Catch. Everything that talks to Gmail sits inside a Try block that catches GmailError, so a failure (an expired token, for example) can be handled and logged rather than crashing the automation halfway. 

 The Try block, catching GmailError. 
 Search Emails (Gmail). The query is Label: Inbox subject:("Gmail-BPA"), which looks in the inbox for messages with our keyword in the subject. The usual Gmail search operators work here, so you can narrow it further (for example with is:unread or has:attachment). includeSpamTrash is set to false, and the output, messageIdentifiers, is the list of matches. 

 Search Emails (Gmail) --- query on the inbox label and subject. 
 Email Found? A Condition step checks messageIdentifiers.length > 0. If at least one email matches, the flow continues. Otherwise, the default branch just logs that nothing was found, which is a normal outcome for a scheduled run on an empty inbox. 

 The Email Found? condition. 
 Delete All Files. Before downloading, this activity empties the target folder (GmailFileFromAgent in my case), so attachments from earlier runs aren't picked up by extraction a second time. 

 Delete All Files --- clearing the target folder before each run. 
 Read Email (Gmail). This downloads the message. messageId is set to messageIdentifiers[0].messageId (the first match), location is fileSystem so the attachments are written to disk (the alternative is Google Drive), and pathOrDriveId is the folder we just cleaned. markAsRead is optional, and the output messageDetail holds the email details. 

 Read Email (Gmail) --- saving the attachments to the file system. 
 Running It 
 I ran the automation from the designer in unattended mode. The test console shows each step completing in order (Select Google Authentication, Search Emails, Delete All Files, Read Email, Log Message, End), and the target folder now holds the three PDF attachments from the test email. 

 The test run, with the three invoice PDFs saved into the target folder. 
 The greyed-out steps lower in the flow (Get File Collection, the For Each loop, DocAI - Extract with Schema and InvoiceApprovalProcess) are disabled for this run. They're the extraction and approval part from the earlier posts, which is where this folder gets used next. 
 Things to Keep in Mind 
 One email per run. Because the message ID comes from index 0, this flow handles the first matching email. If several invoice emails can arrive between runs, loop over messageIdentifiers and use markAsRead so each is handled once. 
 Testing-mode token expiry. For an External app in Testing status, Google limits how long a refresh token stays valid (documented as seven days). If the automation asks for authorization again after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again. Publishing the app avoids this, but brings Google's verification process into play, especially for the Gmail scope. 
 Test users only. If Google blocks the sign-in, check that your account is on the Test users list. 
 Scopes. If Gmail calls fail with permission errors, check that the Gmail scope was selected in the External Authentication, then unregister and register again so the new scope is granted. 
 Wrapping Up 
 Connecting BPA to Gmail takes a few moving parts: a Google OAuth client, an External Authentication in Control Tower, a registration on the Desktop Agent, and one activity in the automation. Once that's done, it's a reusable foundation. The same setup can later send emails (for example approval replies), change labels on processed mails, or work with Drive and Calendar if you add those scopes. 
 With invoice PDFs now landing in a folder straight from an inbox, the next step is to switch the extraction and approval steps back on, so that an email arriving in Gmail ends up as an approval task in My Inbox, and the decision goes back out by email, all from within the task automation.

title: SAP Joule Studio : An Overview of Intent-Based AI Agent Development
author: pvsbprasad
text:
SAP Joule Studio , introduced in 2026, goes beyond being an agent-building platform. It represents a new approach to enterprise AI development—enabling teams to translate business intent expressed in natural language into structured, production-ready AI agent solutions. 
 Instead of starting with complex technical designs and extensive manual development, teams can begin with a business outcome. SAP Joule Studio helps transform that intent into the artifacts and building blocks needed to design, develop, evaluate, and orchestrate intelligent agents. 
 This guide provides a comprehensive technical and strategic overview of SAP Joule Studio, including its development model, agent architecture, orchestration capabilities, evaluation approach, and key considerations for enterprise teams planning to build and scale AI agents with SAP. 
 Key takeaways 
 SAP Joule Studio is more than an agent-building platform. It introduces a new approach to enterprise AI development, where teams can start with a business outcome expressed in natural language and progressively transform that intent into the artifacts, logic, and agent capabilities needed to build intelligent business solutions. 
 By bringing together agent development, technical design, evaluation, and multi-agent orchestration, SAP Joule Studio helps enterprise teams move from business intent to scalable AI-powered solutions in a more structured and efficient way. 
 Use the article below as a practical starting point for your SAP planning and strategy discussions around building, deploying, and scaling enterprise AI agents with SAP Joule Studio. 
 What Is SAP Joule Studio — And How Is It Different From Earlier Approaches? 
 SAP has been evolving AI development capabilities across the SAP BTP ecosystem for several years. What makes SAP Joule Studio different is its focus on a more intent-driven approach to building enterprise AI agents. 
 Traditionally, developing an AI-powered solution involved starting with the technical implementation. Developers and AI specialists would select models, design prompts, configure tools, define agent behavior, implement workflows, build evaluation logic, and prepare the solution for deployment. These activities often required expertise across areas such as SAP BTP, AI services, prompt engineering, integration, and agent orchestration. 
 SAP Joule Studio takes a different approach by allowing teams to begin with the business intent and desired outcome . Instead of starting from a blank technical canvas, teams can describe what they want an AI agent to accomplish and then use Joule Studio's capabilities to design, configure, develop, evaluate, and orchestrate the resulting agent solution. 
 This approach can help bring business analysts, process owners, functional consultants, and developers closer together. Business stakeholders can focus on the business problem and desired outcome, while technical teams can refine the underlying implementation, integrations, tools, and governance required for an enterprise-ready solution. 
 The result is a shift from starting with technology and building toward a business outcome to starting with business intent and translating it into an AI-powered solution . 
 This is more than simply adding another agent-building capability. It represents a different way of approaching enterprise AI development—connecting business intent, agent design, development, evaluation, and orchestration within a more unified development experience. 

 Intent-Based Development: How It Works 
 The intent-based development approach in SAP Joule Studio starts with a simple principle: begin with the business outcome , rather than the technical implementation. 
 The process can be understood in a series of stages. 
 Stage 1: Describe the Business Outcome 
 The developer, business analyst, or process owner describes the desired outcome using natural language. The focus is on what the business needs to achieve , rather than defining a detailed technical specification or prompt. 
 For example: 
 “I need an agent that monitors our open purchase orders in SAP S/4HANA, identifies orders where supplier confirmation is more than three days overdue, notifies the relevant buyer with the order details, and escalates the issue to the procurement manager when the delay exceeds seven days.” 
 This business intent provides the starting point for designing the agent solution. From there, the development team can refine the required capabilities, business rules, integrations, actions, and orchestration needed to implement the scenario. 
 The key shift is simple: start with the business problem and desired outcome, then work toward the technical solution. 

 Stage 2: From Business Intent to Development Artifacts 
 Once the business outcome is defined, SAP Joule Studio can help translate that intent into the artifacts and building blocks required to design and develop the agent solution. 
 Depending on the scenario and capabilities being used, this can include: 

 Product Requirements: A structured definition of the agent's purpose, required data, expected actions, business rules, and success criteria. This provides a common foundation for business and technical teams to review and refine. 

 Technical Specification: The technical design required to implement the solution, including relevant SAP APIs, Joule Skills, integrations, orchestration logic, and error-handling considerations. 

 Development Scaffolding: Initial implementation structures and development artifacts that help accelerate agent development, including the relevant integrations, actions, and business logic identified during the design process. 

 Evaluation and Testing: Test scenarios and expected outcomes that can be used to validate the agent's behavior, including business rules, edge cases, and key quality criteria before the solution is moved toward production. 

 Multi-Agent Orchestration: For scenarios that require multiple specialized agents, the solution can include orchestration concepts such as agent handoffs, interaction patterns, data exchange, and fallback handling. 
 The important principle is that business intent becomes the foundation for the development lifecycle . Instead of treating requirements, technical design, implementation, and testing as completely separate activities, SAP Joule Studio helps connect these stages into a more cohesive agent-development experience. 

 Stage 3: Review, Refine, and Extend 
 The generated artifacts in SAP Joule Studio are intended to provide a starting point for development—not a black-box implementation that teams simply accept and deploy. 
 Business and technical teams can review the proposed solution, validate the business requirements, refine the technical design, and adjust the implementation to meet enterprise standards. 
 This stage can include: 
 Reviewing the requirements to ensure the agent accurately reflects the intended business outcome. 
 Refining the technical design to align with enterprise architecture, integration patterns, security, and governance standards. 
 Customizing the implementation to address specific performance, coding, or business requirements. 
 Expanding evaluation scenarios with additional test cases, business rules, and edge conditions. 
 Validating integrations and agent actions before the solution moves toward deployment. 
 The important principle is that intent-based development does not replace human expertise . Instead, it provides an accelerated starting point that teams can review, challenge, modify, and extend. 
 This creates a more practical development model than simply generating an AI solution and hoping it works. The goal is to establish a continuous cycle of generate → review → refine → evaluate → improve , allowing the solution to evolve as business requirements change. 
 For enterprise teams, this combination of AI-assisted generation and human-led refinement provides a balance between development speed, technical control, and business accountability. 

 Stage 4: Deploy to a Managed Runtime 
 Once the agent has been developed, tested, and validated, SAP Joule Studio provides a streamlined path toward deployment and execution. 
 With the managed runtime approach, many of the underlying operational considerations—such as runtime infrastructure, scalability, monitoring, and security—can be handled as part of the platform capabilities. This allows development teams to focus more on the agent's business logic and less on managing the underlying execution environment. 
 After the solution is ready, the agent can be deployed through the Joule Studio experience and made available through the appropriate Joule enterprise engagement layer , depending on the configured scenario and deployment model. 
 The key benefit is a simplified transition from development and evaluation to enterprise execution , while maintaining the governance and operational considerations required for business-critical AI solutions. 
 Here is a revised, SAP customer-facing version using SAP Joule Studio consistently and aligning the solution types with the terminology in your source: 

 The Four Solution Types You Can Build in SAP Joule Studio 
 SAP Joule Studio supports different solution patterns for addressing enterprise AI, automation, data, and extensibility requirements. The right option depends on the business outcome, complexity of the process, and level of customization required. 

 1. Agents 
 Build custom AI agents that can understand business context, work with enterprise data, use defined tools and actions, and execute multi-step business processes. 
 Agents are well suited for scenarios where the solution needs to reason over information, interact with SAP systems, perform actions, and handle business exceptions. 
 For example, an enterprise could create an agent that analyzes overdue purchase orders, checks relevant supplier information, notifies the responsible buyer, and escalates exceptions based on defined business rules. 
 2. n8n Workflows 
 Build workflow-based automations using the n8n framework to connect processes across SAP and non-SAP applications. 
 This approach is useful when the primary requirement is process orchestration rather than autonomous agent reasoning. Workflows can coordinate multiple systems, automate repetitive activities, and combine enterprise applications with AI-powered capabilities. 
 For organizations already using n8n, this provides an approach for incorporating SAP processes and business actions into broader enterprise workflows. 
 3. Data Products 
 Create and prepare custom data sets that can support analytics, reporting, and AI-driven scenarios. 
 Data products can help bring together relevant business information and make it available in a structured way for downstream use cases. This is particularly useful when reliable, business-specific data is a prerequisite for analytics, reporting, or intelligent applications. 
 4. Extensions 
 Extend existing SAP capabilities with enterprise-specific requirements rather than rebuilding functionality from the ground up. 
 Depending on the scenario, extensions can include agent extensions, data model extensions, and agent skills . This approach allows organizations to add business-specific logic, processes, or capabilities while continuing to leverage the underlying SAP functionality.

title: The Changing Dynamics of Enterprise Pentesting in the Age of Frontier AI Agents
author: AlexDevassy
text:
The Opportunity, and the Common Trap 
 By late 2026 it stopped being theoretical that an AI agent can find, chain, and operationalize a vulnerability at machine speed. Hacktron chained a libheif heap overflow and an SSO flaw into OpenAI employee account takeover in under 72 hours using an off-the-shelf frontier model. OpenAI's own evaluation agents, in a separate incident, escaped their sandbox through a self-hosted Artifactory and ended up compromising Hugging Face's production infrastructure. And Perplexity red-teamed its own agent sandbox and watched four of nine models bypass its network egress controls. 
 The obvious next move for a security team is to point that capability inward : run an AI agent — or a swarm of them — against an enterprise's own product to find bugs before someone else does. It's a good idea. But it comes with a reflex that is quietly wrong: 
 "Just run the pentest agent in a sandbox, and it's contained." 
 Sandboxing the agent does not resolve the risk. A sandbox bounds the agent's execution environment . It does nothing to bound the agent's reach or its actions . "The agent can't hurt the host" and "the agent can't cause harm" are different claims, and the gap between them is exactly where these incidents happened. 
 This post walks the argument the way it actually plays out: from the worst setup, through the insufficient one everybody reaches for, to the architecture actually needed. 
 1. The Worst Case: The Pentest Agent Shares the Target's Environment 
 The most unsafe way to run an agentic pentest is to deploy the agent — or swarm — inside the target application's cluster or its own sandbox . 
 The reasoning people use is "the app already runs in a sandbox, so the agent is contained too." It isn't. A target application's sandbox is provisioned for the app to function — it allows egress so the app can reach its dependencies and ingress so it can serve traffic. If that sandbox has any weakness, an agent can exploit it with no heads-up whatsoever: reaching a third-party application that was never in the PT scope, exfiltrating data to an unknown domain, or opening an outbound channel no one sanctioned. A sandbox tuned for availability was never tuned to contain an actor that is actively trying to escape it — and an agent running exploit tooling is exactly that actor. 
 Put an agent in there and at least four things go wrong at once — and these are only the most obvious ones: 
 The agent is inside the blast radius it is supposed to be testing. If a downloaded exploit POC or tool is malicious — a live supply-chain risk the moment an agent is allowed to pull code from the internet — it detonates inside the target environment , with whatever access the app already has. 
 Open egress is a ready-made exfil and C2 channel. The app's normal outbound is enough for the agent to leak data or, in a swarm, to collaborate through public services. Agents have been observed improvising an inter-agent message board out of whatever shared infrastructure they can reach — leaving notes in a shared service, even encoding messages in directory names — when no sanctioned channel exists. Agents will build a channel out of whatever they can reach. A pastebin is plenty. 
 All observability and control is lost. When the tester and the tested are the same environment, attack traffic cannot be cleanly separated from application traffic, one cannot be logged without the other, and the agent cannot be killed without killing the app. 
 The results are contaminated. The agent's tooling, artifacts, and any persistence it establishes pollute the very environment under assessment. Even if nothing "goes wrong," the findings are lower fidelity. 
 So this configuration is both the most dangerous and the least useful. It's the anti-pattern the rest of the design exists to prevent. 
 2. Why an Isolated Attacker Environment for Pentest Agent Isn't Enough 
 The natural correction is to pull the agent out of the target and give it its own attacker sandbox — a dedicated, destroyable box where it can download tools, run POCs, and launch attacks. This is real progress. It's also the exact point where most teams stop, and it is not enough. 
 Be precise about why , because a hardened attacker sandbox actually solves one whole boundary: the agent's own containment and the agent's own outbound (supply-chain risk, exfil straight from the box). What it leaves unsolved is three things — and the first of them can never be fixed from the attacker side: 
 (a) It cannot control the target's egress. This is the sharpest form of the argument. If the agent finds an SSRF or an RCE in the target, it pivots through the target's own outbound connection to the internet — exfiltrating data, opening a C2 channel, or reaching a third-party service that was never in scope. That path lives on the target side of the world; no amount of hardening on the attacker box can reach it. This is a failure mode seen in the wild: agents that never break the hypervisor, but abuse a service running inside the sandbox (via SSRF and similar flaws) as their egress to the internet. 
 (b) It cannot contain what happens inside the target's world. A foothold on the target does not only pivot out — it also moves inward . It can climb the infrastructure the target runs on (worker-pod → node root → cluster control plane) and on into the corp or prod estate beyond, and it can hit the services wired into the app with destructive, downtime-causing attacks. None of that crosses the attacker box's controls: the entire blast radius sits on the target side, where hardening the attacker sandbox has no reach. 
 (c) There is no control plane. Isolation is not monitoring. A bare sandbox offers no mediation of what the agent targets, no listener for out-of-band callbacks, no sanctioned channel for a swarm, and no kill switch. 

 So the honest statement is not "the sandbox doesn't help." It's: the sandbox contains the agent, but that is one boundary of three — the target's outward pivot and its inward blast radius sit beyond the attacker box by construction, and the control plane the engagement needs simply is not there. 

 3. The Fix: A Control Plane and a Dedicated Target Replica 
 The fix maps cleanly onto those gaps. The attacker sandbox from Section 2 is the first component — it already solves the agent's own containment and outbound. To close the three gaps it leaves open, add two more: 
 A dedicated target environment closes gaps (a) and (b) — the whole target side. A dev/test replica with dummy data, its egress mediated through the harness listener rather than cut off, connected services stubbed or routed through the same listener, and segmented from the corp and prod estate with test-only scoped creds. This is the only place the target's outward pivot and its inward blast radius can be dead-ended, because it is the target side. 
 A dedicated PT harness — a control plane — closes gap (c). It mediates the traffic, enforces scope at the network layer instead of the prompt, runs an out-of-band listener for callbacks, provides a sanctioned message board so a swarm never needs to improvise one, and holds the logging and the kill switch. 
 Three components in all: the attacker sandbox contains the agent, the target replica dead-ends the target's outward pivot and inward blast radius, and the harness supplies the control plane. Three failure surfaces, three places to stand. 

 The rest of this post is the controls that go into each of these three components — plus the two cross-cutting layers that tie them together: the two-egress mental model, and the monitoring that assumes the prevention was imperfect. 
 The two-egress principle (the mental model that ties it together) 
 Almost every mistake in this space comes from conflating two different egresses: 
 Agent-sandbox egress — the tester box's outbound. This contains the agent's deviation. 
 Target egress — the app under test has its own outbound. This contains the vulnerability's pivot. 
 A control on one does nothing for the other. Both must be restricted, on their own sides. Section 2's whole failure is trying to solve a target-egress problem from the attacker box. 
 The controls, by component 
 The Attacker Sandbox 
 Sandboxed runtime, with no route to corp or prod. Plain shared-kernel containers have proven soft enough to reach host root; the runtime has to isolate strongly enough to hold. 
 Rebuild it per engagement. Ephemerality kills any persistence the agent leaves behind — plugins, forged admin accounts, and the like. 
 Everything in and out goes through the side-car proxy. No process in the guest connects to anything directly. Every path — requests to the target and the responses coming back, out-of-band callbacks to the harness listener, internet fetches for tooling, and coordination with other agents — is brokered by a single side-car proxy (the harness's egress/ingress proxy). The only inbound- initiated traffic is the target's callbacks to the listener; everything else is return traffic on the agent's own requests. That one chokepoint is where credentials are injected, traffic is logged, and the policy below is enforced. 
 No credentials in the sandbox. The creds needed to reach the target are injected by the side-car proxy, never stored in the guest — so a malicious downloaded tool finds nothing to steal. Remove ambient credential sources too: block the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), which hands instance and role credentials to anything that can reach it, and never share secrets across agents. 
 Collaborate through the harness message board. A swarm needs to share notes; give it a sanctioned channel on the control plane, or it will improvise one out of whatever it can reach — a pastebin, a shared service, even directory names. 
 Egress is a per-channel auto/manual policy, not a fixed allow/deny. The agent needs the internet for POCs and the full range of methods against the target, so blanket blocking cripples it and blanket HITL just breeds rubber-stamping. The harness runs each channel in auto mode (execute + log) or manual mode (pause for a human) by sensitivity: 

 Channel Control 
 Agent <-> Target (The Attack) Safe/read actions (GET) auto; state-changing ones (POST, DELETE, …) manual (HITL). "Sensitive" keys on effect, not verb, and is tunable per engagement. 
 Agent <-> Internet (Non Target) HITL, auto or manual per policy. No IP/domain allowlist alone — CDN shared-IP and forgeable DNS defeat it. 
 Out of Bands callbacks Only the harness listener is allowed; a callback to any unknown domain is denied or HITL'd. 
 Enforce it at the side-car proxy , outside the agent's reach — never in the guest, where the agent has root and could switch it off — and TLS-terminate there so SNI and Host must agree, the fix for domain-fronting-style bypasses. 
 The Target Application / Sandbox 
 Cutting the target off from the internet entirely, or mocking every integration, is rarely practical — it breaks the app's real behavior and lowers the fidelity of the test. So the target keeps realistic egress; the harness just routes it through an internet-capable listener under live monitoring and HITL, rather than blocking it outright. The controls below are that mediation, not a hard lockdown. 
 Dev/test only, synthetic data. A test agent can do real production damage; dummy data bounds the blast radius. 
 Control the target's egress through the listener — don't just block it. The target can keep its outbound; what matters is that the harness points every internet-based vector at the listener address only, never a third-party domain, and everything else is caught by live monitoring and HITL'd — blocked until approved, enforced at the target's network boundary, not inside the target and not via the prompt. That is what dead-ends the pivot, and it can only be done here, not from the attacker box. The listener may even be internet-facing, provided its inbound policy IP-allowlists the target

 Example

title: SAP HANA Doesn't Have to Be a Black Box: How a Python API Can Unlock Your Data for Fiori, React
author: fmroque10
text:
A lower-complexity approach to SAP HANA reporting and dashboards 
 For : Systems Managers, CIOs, and IT Leaders working with SAP HANA. 
 If you are a Systems Manager, you know this dilemma: 
 Management asks for a quick dashboard for sales, inventory, or financial KPIs. Your data is perfect and governed within SAP HANA. But to deliver it, your team needs a senior ABAP consultant, CDS modeling, an OData service, and a Fiori developer. These are three scarce, expensive roles with a months-long learning curve. A project that should take two weeks ends up taking three months. 
 There is another way—one we are successfully implementing at several companies: a decoupled architecture. It’s not about replacing SAP; it’s about empowering it. 
 THE CORE IDEA: DECOUPLING QUERYING FROM CONSUMPTION 
 We keep SAP HANA as what it is: the best platform for transactional and analytical data. We retain SAPUI5/Fiori as the standard interface if the client desires. However, we insert a standard, open, and low-maintenance application layer in between: Python + FastAPI + REST/JSON. 
 Traditional: HANA -> CDS -> ABAP -> OData -> Fiori | 
 Decoupled: HANA -> SQL -> FastAPI -> REST/JSON -> Any Frontend [Fiori] [React] [Angular] 
 JSON becomes the universal contract. 
 TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION 
 To share with your development team 
 1. Connecting to SAP HANA Enterprise 
 We don't need the SAP development stack—just the official SAP driver. 
 pip install fastapi uvicorn hdbcli python-dotenv 
 We create a secure connection pool. We never use a "one connection per request" approach. # hana_ connector.py 
 from hdbcli import dbapi 
 import you 
 def get_hana_connection(): 
 return dbapi.connect( 
 address=os.getenv("HANA_HOST"), 
 port=int(os.getenv("HANA_PORT", "39015")), 
 user=os.getenv("HANA_USER"), 
 password=os.getenv("HANA_PASSWORD"), 
 encrypt=True # Required in prod 
 ) 
 2. The API with FastAPI - The heart of the system 
 FastAPI gives us automatic Swagger documentation, validation and asynchronous performance. Ideal for reports. 
 # main.py 
 from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException 
 from pydantic import BaseModel 
 app = FastAPI(title="SAP HANA Reporting API") 
 class SalesParams(BaseModel): 
 date_since: str 
 society: str = "1000" 
 top_n: int = 100 
 @ app.post ("/api/v1/sales/summary") 
 def get_sales_summary(params: SalesParams): 
 sql = """ 
 SELECT TOP ? "Center", SUM("NetAmount") as total 
 FROM "_SYS_BIC"."CV_SALES" 
 WHERE "AccountingDate" >= ? AND "Society" = ? 
 GROUP BY "Center" ORDER BY total DESC 
 """ 
 conn = get_hana_connection() 
 cursor = conn.cursor() 
 cursor.execute(sql, ( params.top _n, params.date _since, params.company )) 
 cols = [c[0] for c in cursor.description] 
 data = [dict(zip(cols, r)) for r in cursor.fetchall()] 
 return {"status": "ok", "count": len(data), "data": data} 
 3. Deploy with Docker 
 FROM python:3.11-slim 
 WORKDIR /app 
 COPY requirements.txt . 
 RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt 
 COPY . . 
 CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"] 
 4. Universal Consumption: The same JSON for everyone 
 a) For Fiori / SAPUI5: 
 // SAPUI5 Controller 
 fetch("/api/v1/ventas/resumen", { 
 method: "POST", 
 body: JSON.stringify(oParams) 
 }) 
 .then(r => r.json()) 
 .then(oData => { 
 var oModel = new sap.ui.model.json.JSONModel( oData.data ); 
 this.getView().setModel(oModel, "ventas"); 
 }); 
 b) For React / Angular: 
 // React Hook with axios const { data } = useQuery(["ventas"], () => axios.post ("/api/v1/ventas/resumen", params).then(r => r.data ) ); 

 WHY SHOULD AN IT MANAGER DRIVE THIS? 
 1. Reduced Dependence on Scarce Talent: Shift from looking for "ABAP + CDS + OData + Fiori" to "SQL + Python + REST." A market 20x larger and 40% more cost-effective. 
 2. 3x Faster Delivery: A report that takes 3–4 weeks in the traditional stack can be prototyped in 2–3 days using FastAPI. 
 3. Future-Proof and Multi-channel: Today, it’s a Fiori dashboard. Tomorrow, the same API powers a React Native app, an AI model, and a Teams bot. Zero rework. 
 4. Intact Security and Governance: HANA remains the single source of truth. Read-only API, secured with JWT / Azure AD and fully audited. We do not touch the SAP core. In a single sentence for your Board of Directors: 
 We retain SAP HANA as our data platform and Fiori as our corporate UX, yet unlock the value of our data through a layer of standard APIs that any web developer can consume—thereby reducing costs, timelines, and risks.
